title: Finding the Number of Visible Mountains
statement:
Each entry `peaks[i] = [xi, yi]` is the top of mountain `i`. A mountain is a right isosceles triangle standing on the x-axis with its right angle at the top: its two sides fall with slopes 1 and -1 from `(xi, yi)` down to the base, which runs from `(xi - yi, 0)` to `(xi + yi, 0)`.

Mountain `i` is *visible* unless its top lies inside some other mountain or on that mountain's outline. In particular, two mountains with the same top hide each other. Return the number of visible mountains.
notes:
## Intuition

Comparing every top with every mountain works in O(n²). The geometry simplifies things: mountain `j` covers top `i` exactly when `yi <= yj - |xi - xj|`, which rearranges to `xj - yj <= xi - yi` and `xi + yi <= xj + yj`. So each mountain is just its base interval `[x - y, x + y]`, and a mountain is hidden exactly when its interval lies inside another one. Sorting the intervals by left end, with wider ones first on ties, means every interval that could contain the current one has already been seen, so only the largest right end so far matters.

## Approach

1. Turn each peak into `[left, right] = [x - y, x + y]`.
2. Sort by `left` ascending and, for equal `left`, by `right` descending.
3. Scan in order, keeping `maxRight`, the furthest right end seen. If `right <= maxRight`, an earlier interval contains this one: skip it.
4. Otherwise it reaches further than everything before, so update `maxRight`. It is visible unless the `next` interval is identical (two equal mountains hide each other; the copy will be skipped by step 3).
5. Count the visible ones.

## Example 1, step by step

The peaks give intervals `[0,4]`, `[3,9]` and `[1,9]`; sorted they are `[0,4]`, `[1,9]`, `[3,9]`. `[0,4]` passes `maxRight = -Infinity`, so `maxRight = 4` and `count = 1`. `[1,9]` reaches past 4: `maxRight = 9`, `count = 2`. `[3,9]` has `right = 9 <= 9`, so it is hidden. The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; the scan is linear.
- Space: O(n) for the intervals.

## Pitfalls

- A top on another mountain's outline is hidden too, so compare with `<=`, not `<`.
- Identical mountains hide each other: neither copy counts, even when nothing else covers them.
- Without the descending tie-break on `right`, a wide interval could come after a narrow one with the same `left` and fail to hide it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `intervals` | each mountain's base `[left, right]`, sorted |
| `left`, `right` | the current mountain's base ends |
| `maxRight` | the furthest right end among the mountains already scanned |
| `next` | the following interval, checked for an exact duplicate |
| `count` | visible mountains found so far |

narration.2: A mountain is fully described by its base: it spans x - y to x + y.
narration.3: Sort by left end, and put the wider interval first when left ends tie, so containers come before what they contain.
narration.6: Visit the intervals in sorted order.
narration.8: Some earlier interval starts no later and ends no earlier, so it covers this top...
narration.11: This mountain reaches further right than any before it.
narration.13: An identical mountain right after it hides it (and is itself hidden by this one)...
narration.16: Nothing covers this top: it is visible.
narration.18: Return the number of visible mountains.
